headline: North Toledo hazmat resolved: evacuation fully lifted Oct. 23, all-clear issued at MC Tank Transport — cleanup under US EPA oversight
paragraphs: Toledo Fire & Rescue and Lucas County EMA issued an evacuation order for all residents and businesses within one mile of 1050 Progress Ave — the Sterling Pipe & Tube facility in north Toledo — after a hazardous material release was reported at approximately 10:48 PM Tuesday, October 21, 2026. An initial half-mile-radius evacuation order was quickly expanded to a one-mile radius as the chemical plume moved through the area. The Raintree Village mobile home park and the Alexis Addition neighborhood fall within the evacuation zone. Toledo Fire officials confirmed a chemical was detected in the air; its identity was not disclosed in overnight reporting. The plume reduced visibility on roadways throughout the north Toledo area and officials urged drivers to use caution. 13abc reported the incident as it unfolded before midnight on October 21.

The Red Cross and TARTA buses staged at a Meijer on East Alexis to transport evacuating residents. As of initial reporting, no injuries or fatalities were announced. The Sterling Pipe & Tube plant at 1050 Progress Ave is a steel pipe and tube manufacturer in Toledo's north industrial corridor, near Enterprise Boulevard and Progress Avenue. Cause of the chemical release, the specific substance involved, and the timeline for lifting the evacuation order had not been publicly announced at the time of the initial overnight report.

Toledo Fire & Rescue, the Ohio EPA, and Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz provided updated information on October 21 as the response continued into Wednesday. The source was confirmed as the MC Tank Transport terminal at approximately 1266 Progress Ave. — not the Sterling Pipe & Tube facility at 1050 Progress Ave. that initial reports named; Sterling Pipe & Tube director of operations Randy Sprow told WTOL that his facility does not have the chemicals involved on-site. The chemical was identified as glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial compound used in coatings and plastics manufacturing; the Ohio EPA described it as not highly toxic but capable of causing eye, skin, and lung irritation, and characterized it as a potential carcinogen. The Ohio EPA said the release resulted from an 'error that occurred when the material was being transferred' from a 5,500-gallon tank. No explosion occurred, despite some early media characterizations; the tank was venting and officials expected the process to take an additional 6 to 16 hours from approximately 5 PM on October 21. By the afternoon update on October 21, the evacuation zone was reduced from one mile to a half-mile radius — approximately 300 residents still displaced, down from approximately 1,000 — and the three-mile shelter-in-place order was fully lifted. One Lucas County sheriff's deputy was injured with eye and throat irritation and drove himself to a hospital; no other injuries or fatalities were reported. Toledo Public Schools and Washington Local Schools canceled classes on October 21; the City of Toledo treated the day as a 'Level III snow emergency' for employee purposes. City officials confirmed the water supply is unaffected. The venting timeline and the half-mile evacuation zone had not been formally lifted in available reporting as of October 22.

By Thursday morning, October 22, the tank had stopped releasing glycidyl methacrylate and the evacuation zone was further reduced to a quarter-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. — a third reduction from the original one-mile perimeter. Toledo Fire & Rescue confirmed hazmat crews could approach the tank for inspection; the US EPA formally took over perimeter air-quality monitoring as the scene transitioned from emergency response to remediation oversight. The shelter-in-place order remained fully lifted. City officials said crews would continue monitoring overnight into Friday, October 23. At least 57 people were treated at area hospitals for symptoms related to the release, with seven still receiving treatment Thursday afternoon — none in serious condition. Toledo Public Schools and Washington Local Schools reopened on Thursday, October 22, following the cancellations on October 21. Toledo Fire & Rescue characterized the incident as still 'active' as of the afternoon update on October 22, with the quarter-mile evacuation zone in effect and remediation planning underway.

On Friday morning, October 23, the evacuation order around MC Tank Transport was fully lifted. Federal and local authorities confirmed no detectable hazards remained at the site; crews determined conditions were safe for turnover to the company owners and the U.S. EPA for the next phase of cleanup. Mayor Kapszukiewicz confirmed the cause as an employee introducing an inappropriate temperature level while attempting to transfer the liquid glycidyl methacrylate — triggering a chemical reaction — and stated that MC Tank Transport had accepted responsibility. There was no fire and no explosion. The preliminary air monitoring data released by the city showed no readings above threshold levels in the surrounding area. The immediate public safety emergency that began the night of October 21 is resolved; US EPA and Ohio EPA oversight of remediation at 1266 Progress Ave. continues.

As of October 24, 2026, the Ohio EPA investigation into the employee transfer error at MC Tank Transport remains pending; no enforcement findings or timeline have been publicly announced. 13abc reported the business impact on nearby proprietors: Skyline Party Rentals, located within the evacuation zone, faces cleanup costs and lost employee pay as a direct result of the multi-day disruption. The economic toll on small businesses along the Progress Avenue corridor — separate from the 57 people treated at hospitals — is an emerging accountability dimension of the incident beyond its immediate public safety resolution.

Two proposed class-action lawsuits have been filed in Lucas County Common Pleas Court over the October 20–23 glycidyl methacrylate release. The first, filed October 23 by Toledo business owner Todd Hartford and his landscaping company, names MC Tank Transport, parent company Kenan Advantage Group, and plant manager Albert Dudek as defendants; claims include negligence, gross negligence/recklessness, nuisance, and strict liability for an abnormally dangerous activity. The second suit, filed October 26 by north Toledo resident Mallory Van Camp — who lives approximately 2.5 miles from the terminal — names MC Tank Transport, Kenan Advantage Group, and KAG Leasing, and asserts seven claims including negligence, nuisance, strict liability, and trespass. Both suits allege the company failed to maintain adequate levels of a chemical inhibitor designed to prevent unwanted reactions and failed to properly monitor and control the tank's temperature and pressure. Counsel for the plaintiffs estimates the proposed class could number in the thousands, covering residents forced to evacuate and businesses forced to close or limit operations within three miles of 1266 Progress Ave. The two cases have been assigned to separate judges in Lucas County Common Pleas Court and could eventually be consolidated; neither class has been certified. Separately, MC Tank Transport and parent Kenan Advantage Group have launched a claims process for North Toledo neighbors seeking compensation for chemical-leak-related costs — WTOL reported on the process as of October 28, 2026.

Attorneys representing plaintiffs in the proposed class-action suits are warning North Toledo neighbors to review claim paperwork carefully before accepting compensation payments from Kenan Advantage Group. 13abc reported October 30 that attorneys have advised residents that signing claim documents from the company could waive their future legal rights to pursue additional damages through the litigation process — including potential damages sought in the class actions. The warning creates a direct tension between the company's voluntary claims process, intended to address immediate out-of-pocket costs, and the pending lawsuits alleging negligence and strict liability. Residents who sign releases without legal counsel may forgo recovery in the class actions even if one or both suits are ultimately certified and succeed.
why_it_matters: The MC Tank Transport glycidyl methacrylate release — which displaced up to 1,000 north Toledo residents, closed schools in two districts, sent 57 people to hospitals, and drew national media coverage — ended with a full all-clear on October 23. The incident confirmed two persistent vulnerabilities: the industrial-residential interface in Toledo's north Progress Avenue corridor, and the gap between initial emergency characterizations (explosion reports, misidentified source facility) and verified facts. The Ohio EPA investigation into the employee transfer error is the remaining accountability thread: regulatory findings and any enforcement action against MC Tank Transport will set the precedent for how Ohio oversees chemical transfer operations at industrial terminals near residential areas. This is the second major industrial safety event in Toledo in 2026, after the Brent Industries explosion in south Toledo in August.
